before.exam_tip_html: In the exam, the Prologue is a powerful quotation bank for almost any question on the play. If asked about fate, conflict, or love, you can use it. Always analyse why Shakespeare reveals the ending — focus on dramatic irony and its effect on the audience. Examiners reward students who connect context (Elizabethan beliefs about fate) to the writer’s methods (the sonnet form, the word “star-cross’d”).

In an extract question, always link your analysis back to context. For example, if a question asks about Hyde’s appearance, connect the animalistic language to Victorian fears about degeneration and Darwin. Examiners reward answers that show understanding of why Stevenson made specific choices, not just what those choices are.

When writing about the opening chapters, focus on Stevenson’s use of withholding as a structural device. Examiners want to see that you understand why Stevenson delays the revelation — it builds suspense and forces the reader to share Utterson’s growing unease.

When analysing the shared sonnet (Act 1, Scene 5), always comment on form as well as language. The fact that Romeo and Juliet complete each other’s lines shows their connection. Examiners reward students who can explain why Shakespeare chose a sonnet here — it links their meeting to the Prologue (also a sonnet) and to the tradition of love poetry, while foreshadowing that their love is inseparable from their fate.

When analysing ambition, always link Macbeth’s choices to Shakespeare’s purpose. Why does Shakespeare give us “brave Macbeth” before showing his dark side? Because the tragedy is more powerful when a good man falls. In your essay, show how Shakespeare constructs Macbeth’s journey from hero to villain — the examiner wants to see that you understand the playwright’s craft, not just the plot.

Act 3 is the most commonly examined section of the play. If you get an extract from this act, focus on the turning point — how Shakespeare shifts from comedy to tragedy. Always analyse Romeo’s line “O, I am fortune’s fool!” in terms of the fate vs free will debate. Examiners reward students who explore multiple interpretations rather than settling for one simple reading.

When writing about Jekyll and Hyde, avoid the common mistake of treating them as completely separate characters. Examiners want to see that you understand they are two sides of the same person. Use Jekyll’s own quotation — “man is not truly one, but truly two” — to anchor your argument.

When writing about character in the exam, avoid simply describing what a character does. Instead, analyse how Doyle presents them (AO2) and why (AO3). For Holmes, discuss the tension between genius and self-destruction. For Mary, explore how she both challenges and conforms to Victorian gender norms. For Small, argue whether he is a villain or a victim. The examiner rewards nuanced analysis, not plot retelling.

Questions about Utterson are really questions about Victorian values. Show how his loyalty, discretion and rationality both protect and endanger Jekyll. Link his refusal to pry to the wider theme of repression. Examiners want to see that you understand characters as vehicles for Stevenson’s ideas.

For the 30-mark essay on Stave 5, compare similes across staves to show structural awareness. Always link Scrooge’s actions in Stave 5 back to specific moments in Stave 1 to demonstrate understanding of the cyclical structure. Include Dickens’s social purpose — the examiner rewards answers that explain why Dickens wrote the novella, not just what happens in it. Use phrases like “Dickens intends the reader to…” or “Dickens uses this to convey his message that…”

When writing about Act 5, always address the dramatic irony of Romeo not knowing Juliet is alive. Examiners reward students who can explain why Shakespeare makes the audience watch a preventable tragedy — it forces them to feel the devastating consequences of the feud, secrecy, and impulsiveness. Compare Romeo’s elaborate death speech with Juliet’s brief, decisive action to analyse gender presentation.

When writing about supporting characters, always explain their function in the play as a whole. Examiners want to see that you understand why Shakespeare includes them. Mercutio is a foil to Romeo; Tybalt personifies the feud; the Nurse represents the failure of the adult world. Use the term “foil” in your answer — it demonstrates sophisticated literary understanding.

In the AQA exam you answer one essay question on Animal Farm, chosen from two. You write about the whole novella, closed book, with no extract printed. Always link Orwell’s methods to his purpose — examiners reward answers that explain why Orwell made particular choices, not just what happens. Use the phrase “Orwell uses [technique] to [effect] in order to [purpose]” as a structural frame.
